title: Northeast Kansas education board candidates share ideas for funding, local control, technology
description: TOPEKA — While the Democrat running for the Kansas State Board of Education’s northeast district wants the state to fully fund special education, the Republican candidate says the board should investigate spending first. text:
Democrat Jennifer Lloyd, left, and Republican Amy Cawvey will oppose each other in the November general election to represent Kansas' northeastern corner on the Kansas State Board of Education. (Kansas Reflector composite from photos submitted by the candidates)TOPEKA — While the Democrat running for the Kansas State Board of Education’s northeast district wants the state to fully fund special education, the Republican candidate says the board should investigate spending first.
The Legislature has not met its obligation to fund 92% of special education costs since the 2010-2011 school year, according to the Kansas State Department of Education, which estimated the state fell short of its obligation this current fiscal year by $226 million. In May, four Johnson County school districts announced plans to sue the state for the deficit.
Democrat Jennifer Lloyd, of Ozawkie, and Republican Amy Cawvey, of Lansing, disagree about funding plans. But they both hope to support local control and limit digital technology — in different ways.
Lloyd said fully funding special education is vital.
“Not funding the special ed is what is causing so much crisis in all of the schools, in public schools right now,” she said. “We’re having to use general funds to cover special ed, and then that’s pulling away from all of the kids.”
Cawvey said she has seen schools throw the budget “out the window” and wants to audit special education spending records.
“Yes, it will cost taxpayer dollars,” she said. “But I think it would be well worth it before we just say we need more money.”
 
The candidates
Lloyd, a librarian at Jefferson West School District, grew up attending Jefferson County public schools and earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in education and library science at Emporia State University. Before becoming a librarian, she taught special education and fifth grade in the same northeast state board district.
Financially supporting teachers is central to her candidacy.
“Our teachers are spending so much money, their own money,” and then not getting the pay raises that they need to be able to keep doing this,” she said.
Jennifer Lloyd, right, campaigns at a community event in Oskaloosa. (Photo submitted by Jennifer Lloyd)
Cawvey volunteers as the Kansas chair of the National School Boards Coalition and previously served on the Lansing school board. Years ago, her husband’s role in the military moved their family to several states across the country, including Hawaii. Wherever they went, she said, she volunteered at her children’s schools as a substitute teacher or in parent-teacher organizations.
She said her experiences in diverse school districts gave her insight into school systems.
“We were in some poor school districts and some districts that had more money,” she said. “We just did the best with what we had and got to know the staff and everyone.”
Amy Cawvey, right, campaigns at a Republican convention. (Photo submitted by Amy Cawvey)
The northeast district Lloyd and Cawvey aim to represent is one of the state board’s 10 districts. Five seats are up for reelection this year. All five Republican incumbents declined to seek reelection. Because Democrats hold the majority of the other five seats, Kansas voters could switch the board’s GOP majority.
 
Local control
The state board oversees Kansas K-12 public schools while working with local school districts — responsible for applying the state board’s standards — and the Legislature — responsible for state funding.
Both candidates said they want to maintain local control by improving the state board’s coordination with the Legislature, which considered bills in the 2026 session to impose certain curricula, such as lessons on communism and an annual fitness test.
Gov. Laura Kelly vetoed those bills, but she signed one to bar students from using their cellphones at school. The law requires districts to securely store students’ phones without providing funding for a storage method.
While both candidates said cellphone policies work best under local control, they disagree about the ban.
Cawvey said lawmakers got involved because local districts and the state board failed to set effective rules.
“It was implemented some at a local level, but then it wasn’t consistent,” she said. “The state board in the middle also needs to work. And they didn’t issue a lot of guidance on that either. They didn’t do as much as I felt they could.”
Lloyd said the Legislature’s ban prevented the state board from setting a cellphone standard.
“Instead of letting the schools, the state board having a recommendation and coming down to the local level, the local levels are now having to react,” she said. “So it’s causing some financial burdens on some of the districts to handle the cellphone ban.”
 
Digital technology
Both candidates want to address technology in the classroom if elected by limiting young students’ access to screens and making recommendations to schools soon.
Specifically, Lloyd said the state board should set standards regarding the one to one student device ratio schools implemented during COVID-19 and have continued.
“The local levels are spending money on technology, and so we need to get ahead of that and make sure the local boards see where the state board is,” Lloyd said.
Those recommendations by the state board, she said, should limit younger students’ access to technology in a way that transitions into greater access as students get older.
Cawvey wants to limit screens for all students. And, she said, local districts and state board should address technology soon before the state does.
“I would suggest,” Cawvey said, “if I was on a local board now, to go ahead and start implementing that now, because that’s kind of what happened with the cellphones.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Judge promises quick decision on challenge to Missouri property tax caps
description: A Cole County judge said Wednesday he will rule quickly on a case that will determine if property tax caps voted on in April take effect later this year. At the end of a three-hour hearing, Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh gave attorneys in the case one week to file proposed findings for him to consider. […]
text:
The Cole County Courthouse in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)A Cole County judge said Wednesday he will rule quickly on a case that will determine if property tax caps voted on in April take effect later this year.
At the end of a three-hour hearing, Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh gave attorneys in the case one week to file proposed findings for him to consider. The case needs quick attention, Limbaugh told the attorneys, because he may be given post-primary election cases that will require fast action.
Taxing jurisdictions need a ruling as well, Limbaugh was told, because local boards must hold public hearings in August to set tax rates as the next step in preparing this year’s property tax notices.
The property tax provisions being challenged in the lawsuit before Limbaugh were included in the bill lawmakers passed last year diverting state tax revenue to support stadium construction for the Kansas City Chiefs and Royals. 
The property tax provisions were a demand from rural lawmakers reluctant to provide more than $1 billion in tax support for professional sports teams.
In a late night session, the state Senate added provisions directing 97 of Missouri’s 114 counties to place questions on their April ballots asking voters if they wanted to limit increases in property tax bills. 
For 22 of those counties, the question was whether they wanted to freeze residential tax bills, with exceptions for new voter-approved taxes and debt service levies. For the other 75, the question was whether to enact a cap, set at 5% or the rate of inflation, whichever is greater.
The lawsuit heard Wednesday was filed by a taxpayer from St. Louis, which was excluded from the law, one from Warren County, which was in the zero growth group, and seven taxing districts. The lawsuit was joined by county commissions from 43 counties.
The lawsuit contends the portions of the bill containing the property tax caps and freezes violate the Missouri Constitution. The counties designated for a cap or freeze are described based on population and each provision is a special local law, the plaintiffs argued Wednesday.
There is no rational basis for why any county is given the designation it received, attorney Natalie Ann Hoernschemeyer said.
“There is absolutely no pattern,” she said. “It is absolutely random.”
Attorneys for the state, defending the law, said the designations mostly put counties where assessment updates are needed into the category that gives the most protection.
The Missouri State Tax Commission grades each county on how close its residential and commercial property assessments are to market value. It pressures counties that lag into updating the values, which can bring unwelcome and surprising increases in property tax bills.
Not every county designation is perfect and deciding if there is a rational basis for the designations in the bill does not require perfection, said Sean McDowell, assistant attorney general. 
“The idea that we are just advocating for the policy interests of the General Assembly is wrong,” he said.
If Limbaugh rules in favor of the plaintiffs, it will only impact the enforceability of the property tax provisions of the stadium bill. While the Chiefs have decided to move to Kansas, the Royals are pressing forward with plans for a new ballpark in Missouri.
In a separate case challenging the constitutionality of the stadium subsidies, Limbaugh ruled in January that state Sen. Mike Moon of Ash Grove, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin of Ste. Genevieve and conservative activist Ron Calzone did not have standing — the legal right to sue.
They argued that the stadium bill was an unconstitutional grant of state resources to a private entity and improperly combined widely different and unrelated subjects.
Calzone, Moon, and Wolfin are appealing the dismissal. The Missouri Supreme Court will hear arguments in the appeal on Sept. 1.
Not every county directed to hold an election did so, court filings in the case show.
Of the 97 counties listed in the legislation:

One, Texas County, placed it on the November ballot and it passed.
23 counties directed to hold a vote under the legislation did not do so.
61 counties enacted the cap in April, 14 designated for tax bill freezes and 47 with the 5% cap.
12 counties voted against the ballot measure, five designated for a tax freeze and seven that would have had the 5% cap.

Much of Wednesday’s arguments focused on the fine details of state tax law and how taxes are governed under the Constitution. 
The state legislature is not supposed to enact any laws granting homestead exemptions from property taxes without making restitution to local taxing districts for any lost revenue. In court, the attorneys argued over whether that meant future revenue that would not be collected as a result of the law or whether it meant the taxing districts had to show an actual decline.
The law granting the freeze or cap does not have any provision regarding restitution.
The arguments also focused on whether the legislation created an impermissible new subclassification of property — owner-occupied residences — in the law.
The Constitution promises uniformity of taxation for all property within a taxing district, said Jim Layton, attorney for the taxing districts. 
“This is actually the simplest legal analysis on which to resolve this case,” he said.
The bill did not create a new subclass of property, McDowell said. The Constitution promises uniformity of tax rates on particular types of property and the bill does not change tax rates, he said.
The counties that joined the lawsuit object to being forced to bear the cost of the April election, attorney Travis Elliott told Limbaugh. That is a violation of the Hancock Amendment’s ban on legislation that imposes new duties on local governments without providing the funding necessary to perform the function, he said.
And, he said, the counties agree that it violates the ban on special or local laws. Each provision uses the general phrase “any county” before using a description based on population characteristics that limit the actual application to a single county.
“That’s not a general law,” Elliott said. “That’s county-specific legislation wearing a population classification costume.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Democrats re-introduce nine bills blocked by Hall and vetoed by Whitmer
description: Legislative Democrats in the state House and Senate announced Wednesday they are re-introducing the nine bills that were the center of a lawsuit, a state Supreme Court decision and eventually a veto from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in mid-July.  The bills, which passed both chambers of the legislature in 2024, when Democrats had a trifecta, were […]
text:
Michigan House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said he was "skeptical" of the willingness of House Republican leadership to move forward with the progress of the nine bills, but that Democrats would re-introduce the bills as many times as necessary. July 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Legislative Democrats in the state House and Senate announced Wednesday they are re-introducing the nine bills that were the center of a lawsuit, a state Supreme Court decision and eventually a veto from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in mid-July. 
The bills, which passed both chambers of the legislature in 2024, when Democrats had a trifecta, were never transmitted to Whitmer’s desk for her signature prior to the end of that legislative session, and House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Twp.) refused to do so once he took control of the chamber at the start of 2025. That led to an 18-month legal battle between the leaders in both chambers, which culminated in the Supreme Court declining to take up the case, leaving a Court of Appeals decision in place that ruled it was unconstitutional for Hall not to transmit the bills to the governor’s desk.
Hours after the Supreme Court’s decision, Whitmer vetoed the bills, a decision that legislators and labor leaders alike called a betrayal. 
Now, legislators are bringing the bills back up, though they face an uphill battle in the Republican-controlled House. Hall’s refusal to transmit the initial versions of the bills leads most to expect that he will not push the legislation through his chamber while he remains at its helm.
House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said that, while he hopes to get these bills passed in the last five months of the current legislative session by “holding Republicans’ feet to the fire in the House,” he would join legislators in re-introducing the bills as many times as needed to — including next session, when Democrats hope to reclaim control of the House — in order to get them passed.
“I have not had conversations with the House Republicans on this, but the offer stands that we are willing to work in good faith to get this done,” Puri said. “I’m skeptical if that’s really going to happen in this year. But you know, the alternative to that is making sure that they don’t need to be a part of the equation in 2027.”
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) is surrounded by Democratic senators and representatives, as well as labor leaders, to announce the re-introduction of the nine bills that were the subject of a state court case and led to a veto from Gov. Whitmer. July 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren), who was one of the most vocal critics in the legislature of Whitmer’s decision to veto the bills, said she believes some rank-and-file House Republicans want to see these bills passed, and hopes that party leadership will be willing to work with them. 
“Anything is possible. We are all up for re-election,” Xiong said. “Certainly I look forward to hearing their response because now the ball is in their court, and if they want to take their ball home and not play, then they’re not doing the job that they were elected to do. That sends a very clear message to Michigan families.”
At a press conference on Wednesday morning, legislative Democrats were more focused on Hall’s role in keeping the bills from being passed, rather than Whitmer’s. 
Xiong noted that she hopes Whitmer will be willing to work with legislators on updated versions of the legislation. 
When asked if she believed that Whitmer would sign the bills, should they come to her desk, Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said that she had been confident in the past and could not speculate on the Governor’s intentions. “At this point, she is requesting those bills to come to her desk, and as we are introducing them today, we will make the necessary changes so that they meet the muster,” Brinks said. “We believe that they merit her signature. But that ultimately, as we all know, is a decision that she must make.”
A spokesperson for Whitmer’s office said in response to a question about whether or not she would sign the bills, should they make it to her desk again, “As the governor said, she stands ready to work with the legislature to consider new versions.”
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the frontrunner for the Democrats in the 2026 gubernatorial election, said in a press release following Whitmer’s veto that she would sign the bills into law if elected.
The importance of the bills, which include a shield for working families against debt collection practices that seize tax returns made possible by the Earned Income Tax Credit and a measure preventing massive healthcare costs for teachers and school employees, first responders, nurses and other public servants, was emphasized throughout the press conference. 
“For too long, the people of Michigan, the people who make Michigan run, the people who keep our children safe and educated, our communities healthy, and our state moving have been left to shoulder the burden of rising costs and economic uncertainty alone,” Michigan AFL-CIO President Ron Bieber said. “Michigan’s labor movement is committed to doing whatever is necessary to pass the bills reintroduced today by our friends in the House and Senate, these aren’t just pieces of legislation. These are lifelines for working families.”
